answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: CareSource delegates the prior authorization and clinical reviews of musculoskeletal procedures (including knee arthroscopy/meniscus surgery under CPT code 29881) to TurningPoint Healthcare Solutions, LLC. The governing clinical guidelines are proprietary and not directly published on the public CareSource website. To obtain the exact medical necessity criteria used: 1. The provider can log into the TurningPoint Provider Portal at www.myturningpoint-healthcare.com under the POLICIES section. 2. The provider or patient can contact the TurningPoint Provider Relations team directly by phone at (304) 603-4673 (local West Virginia) or (855) 578-7350 (toll-free), or via email at providersupport@turningpoint-healthcare.com. 3. The patient can call CareSource Member Services at 1-833-230-2099 (TTY: 711) and request a written copy of the specific clinical criteria applied to their denial (Reference number: POC-C29C7CFC4D-26579).
answer.notes: CareSource has outsourced prior authorizations and clinical necessity reviews for orthopedic surgeries to TurningPoint Healthcare Solutions. TurningPoint uses proprietary clinical guidelines (such as Policy OR-1029 for Knee Arthroscopy). Because the denial specifically states 'the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity,' the patient's appeal should focus on providing clear imaging reports (such as an MRI showing a symptomatic meniscal tear), documenting physical exam findings (like a positive McMurray or Apley test, or mechanical symptoms such as locking/giving way), and documenting the failure of conservative treatment trials (such as physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, or activity modification) if applicable.

MUSCULOSKELETAL AND CARDIAC SURGICAL PROCEDURES CareSource ® covers both musculoskeletal and cardiac surgeries for our members. Orthopedic, Neuro-Spine and Cardiac providers can access the following tools to help them provide efficient and quality care. Policies Providers can view clinical guidelines being used by CareSource at www.myturningpoint-healthcare.com . Providers will initially be asked to “Register for Access”. Upon registration, providers will be able to log into the provider portal and select the POLICIES section to view and/or download these clinical guidelines as PDF documents. Musculoskeletal and Cardiac procedures will require prior authorization for medical necessity and will be reviewed by TurningPoint Healthcare Solutions, LLC for adherence and consistency with these clinical guidelines, as well as industry standardized rules. The review will include evaluation of services for being experimental and/or investigative, as well as clinical appropriateness based upon patient demographic information. Providers may also request copies of these clinical guidelines directly from TurningPoint by calling their Provider Relations team at the number listed below, or by emailing providersupport@turningpoint-healthcare.com . result.text: Page 1 of 12 Clinical Policy: Knee Arthroscopy Reference Number: PA.CP.MP.OR.1029 Coding Implications Effective Date: 04/01/2020 Last Review Date: NEW POLICY Revision Log See Important Reminder at the end of this policy for important regulatory and legal information. Common Name: Knee Scope Definition: Knee arthroscopy is a surgical procedure that allows doctors to view the knee joint without making a large incision through the skin and other soft tissues. Arthroscopy is used to diagnose and treat a wide range of knee problems. I. Criteria for Inclusion Knee arthroscopy is considered medically necessary for any of the following indications: A. Intra-articular joint pathology indicated by one of the following: 1. Loose or foreign body confirmed by imaging 2. Symptomatic hemangioma 3. Symptomatic plica, confirmed with imaging or physical exam (e.g. positive provocative test, positive Hughston’s), after failure of at least 6 weeks of conservative treatment* 4. Symptomatic discoid meniscus confirmed by imaging and associated with significant pain or mechanical symptoms (locking or giving way) that interfere with daily activities 5. Chronic knee pain or effusion that meets all of the following: a. Unknown etiology for symptoms after investigation has ruled out other causes b. Imaging (x-rays, MRI, CT) is inconclusive c. Synovial fluid analysis after arthrocentesis is inconclusive or not indicated d. One of the following indications is present: i. Failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* ii. Presence of mechanical symptoms indicating internal derangement (locking or giving way) B. Imaging-confirmed osteochondral defect for one of the following: 1. Displaced lesion, with or without loose body 2. Nondisplaced lesion in skeletally immature individuals (growth plates open) after a failure of at least 12 weeks conservative treatment* 3. Acute nondisplaced lesion in skeletally mature individuals (closed growth plates) 4. Chronic nondisplaced lesion in skeletally mature individuals (closed growth plates) after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* C. Imaging-confirmed articular cartilage defect for one of the following: 1. Acute defect 2. Chronic defect that is symptomatic after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* D. Meniscal tear (see OR-1027 for meniscal repair) confirmed by imaging (where imaging is equivocal, positive McMurray or Apley test can help confirm), for one of the following: 1. Mechanical symptoms indicating internal derangement (locking or giving way) 2. Symptomatic after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* 3. Individual under 18 years of age with large (greater than 10mm) or unstable tear 4. Procedure is coincident with indicated ACL repair or reconstruction E. ACL tear (see OR-1013) CLINICAL POLICY Knee Arthroscopy Page 2 of 12 F. Open or arthroscopic treatment of PCL tear confirmed by imaging or physical exam (positive posterior drawer or posterior sag sign, or reversed pivot shift test) with one of the following: 1. Posterolateral corner injury 2. Presence of concomitant ACL or MCL tear, or avulsion fracture 3. Tibial displacement confirmed on stress radiographs that measures 8mm or more 4. Symptomatic after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* G. Open or arthroscopic treatment of MCL tear or injury indicated by one of the following: 1. Valgus laxity in full extension 2. Presence of concomitant ACL, PCL, or displaced meniscus tear 3. Significant retraction, displacement, or entrapment of ligament 4. Associated patellar dislocation H. Excision of symptomatic Baker’s cyst confirmed by imaging and/or physical exam that is not amenable to treatment with ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* I. Synovectomy for treatment of chronic inflammatory disease or condition, including but not limited to: 1. Rheumatoid arthritis 2. Hemophilic joint disease 3. Pigmented villonodular synovitis J. Debridement, drainage, or lavage for one of the following: 1. Infection 2. Rheumatoid arthritis 3. Arthrofibrosis confirmed by loss of range of motion after prior surgery or trauma, after failure of at least 6 weeks conservative treatment* K. Open or arthroscopic lateral retinacular release for treatment of patellar compression syndrome, confirmed by a positive patella glide or patella tilt test L. Fracture reduction (arthroscopic assist) M. Treatment of arthrofibrosis or patellar clunk syndrome after total knee replacement, confirmed by exam (e.g. limited range of motion, retropatellar crepitus), that has failed to improve with at least 6 weeks of conservative treatment* *Conservative nonsurgical treatments should be documented in the medical records and should include all the following, unless contraindicated: 1. Analgesics or anti-inflammatory medications 2. Physical therapy, or detailed professionally-directed home exercise program 3. Activity modification 4. Weight reduction as appropriate a. For BMI 30 to 35, medical record must document weight discussion b. For BMI 35 or greater, medical record must document plan for weight loss 5. Use of crutches, cane, and/or bracing when appropriate II. Criteria for Exclusion A. Knee arthroscopy is considered not medically necessary for the following: 1. Treatment of osteoarthritis 2. Treatment of meniscal tear in knee with osteoarthritis, unless there are mechanical symptoms (locking, giving way) clearly arising from meniscal tear B. Due to lack of sufficient evidence to establish safety and efficacy, treatment of subchondral/bone marrow lesions and insufficiency fractures is considered investigational (including but not limited to Subchondroplasty®). C. Patients unable or unwilling to cooperate with postoperative rehabilitation. CLINICAL POLICY Knee Arthroscopy Page 3 of 12 D. For persons with significant co-morbidities or complications, the medical record must contain documentation of the risk/benefit of knee arthroscopy. III. Surgical Considerations A. Pre-Operative Considerations: 1. Routine preoperative evaluation 2. Imaging 3. Preoperative treatment, procedures, and stabilization, including: a. Iron supplementation and erythropoietin as indicated b. Ruling out sources of infection, including dental and lower urinary tract infections c. Dental prophylaxis as indicated 4. Preoperative discharge planning as appropriate B. Intra-Operative Considerations: 1. Antibacterial wipes 2. Antibacterial nasal swab C. Post-Operative & Inpatient Considerations: 1. Hospital evaluation and care needs may include: a. Diagnostic test scheduling and completion, including: i. Lower extremity Doppler study 2. Treatment and procedure scheduling and completion, including: i. IV antibiotics ii. DVT prophylaxis iii. Transfusion 3. Consultation, assessment, and other services scheduling and completion, including: a. Physical therapy b. Occupational therapy c. Gait training 4. Monitoring patient's status for deterioration and comorbid conditions; key items include: a. Neurovascular status b. Transfusion need c. Cardiac and respiratory status d. Neuropsychiatric status for delirium, dementia, or confusion e. Nutritional status f. Discharge Planning & Considerations D. Discharge Planning & Considerations 1. Discharge planning includes: a. Assessment of needs and planning for care, including: i. Develop treatment plan (involving multiple providers as needed). ii. Evaluate and address preadmission functioning as needed. iii. Evaluate and address patient or caregiver preferences as indicated. iv. Identify skilled services needed at next level of care, with specific attention to:  Medication management, adherence instruction, and side effects assessment  Pain management  Rehabilitation therapy or equipment coordination  Wound or dressing management v. Evaluate and address psychosocial status issues as indicated b. Early identification of anticipated discharge destination; options include: i. Home, considerations include:  Access to follow-up care  Home safety assessment  Self-care ability, if appropriate CLINICAL POLICY Knee Arthroscopy Page 4 of 12  Caregiver need, ability, and availability ii. Post-acute skilled care or custodial care, as indicated c. Transition of care plan complete, which may include: i. Patient and caregiver education complete ii. Medication reconciliation completion includes:  Compare patient's discharge list of medications (prescribed and over-the-counter) against physician's admission or transfer orders.  Assess each medication for correlation to disease state or medical condition.  Report medication discrepancies to prescribing physician, attending physician, and primary care provider, and ensure accurate medication order is identified.  Provide reconciled medication list to all treating providers.  Confirm that patient, family, or caregiver can acquire medication.  Educate patient, family, and caregiver. 1. Provide complete medication list to patient, family, or caregiver. 2. Confirm that patient, family, or caregiver understands importance of presenting personal medication list to all providers at each care transition, including all physician appointments. 3. Confirm that patient, family, or caregiver understands reason, dosage, and timing of medication (eg, use "teach-back" techniques). iii. Plan communicated to patient, caregiver, and all members of care team, including:  Inpatient care and service providers  Primary care provider  All post-discharge care and service providers iv. Post-discharge appointment plans made as needed, which may include:  Primary care provider  Anticoagulation monitoring  Orthopedic surgeon  Rehabilitation therapy services v. Post-discharge testing and procedure plans made, which may include:  Laboratory testing vi. Referrals made for assistance or support, which may include:  Financial, for follow-up care, medication, and transportation  Community services  Smoking cessation counseling or treatment vii.
